subject: Computing
source: National Curriculum KS2 Computing (sequence, repetition, decomposition, debugging); block-based programming in Scratch following the school's Drive KS2/KS3 Scratch resources

lessons.unit: Unit 1: Programming with sequence and repetition
lessons.title: Algorithms and breaking problems into parts
objectives: Explain what an algorithm is and why it must be precise
Break a big problem into smaller parts (decomposition)
Write a clear algorithm for a familiar task

keywords.def: a precise set of steps to solve a problem
breaking a big problem into smaller parts
exact and clear, with nothing left to guess

starter: Why can't a computer 'guess' what we mean?
Name one job you do that has many steps.

teach.heading: Precise algorithms
bullets: 'Put jam on bread' is vague; 'spread 1 spoon of jam' is precise.
teach.note: Run the classic unplugged challenge: read out vague instructions for drawing a house and have pupils draw on paper, then compare drawings. Then repeat with precise instructions such as 'draw a square 4 cm wide'. Discuss why the results differ.

teach.heading: Decomposition
bullets: A big job is easier in small parts.
Planning a class picnic: invite, food, games, clean up.
Each part is a smaller problem.
teach.note: Ask: how would you plan a class picnic? Draw a tree on screen with four branches. Explain decomposition means breaking the problem down, and that programmers do this for every program.

teach.heading: Decompose a game
bullets: Game: a cat chases a ball.
teach.note: Show this as a diagram on screen. Ask which part they would build first. Stress that we test each small part before putting them together. This prepares them for building in Scratch.

teach.heading: Writing it down
bullets: Check each step with a friend.
teach.note: Model writing the algorithm for 'make a paper aeroplane' as 6 numbered steps. Ask pupils to find any step that is unclear. Misconception: more words always means clearer; clear steps can be short.

practice: Decompose 'cleaning your bedroom' into 4 smaller jobs.
Is this precise? 'Walk to the door.' Make it more precise using steps and a number. (e.g. take 5 steps forward)
Write the first three steps of an algorithm for making a cup of tea or milk.
independent: Write a precise algorithm (6-8 steps) for putting on a coat and fastening it.
Decompose the problem 'make a school newsletter' into at least 4 parts and draw a tree diagram.
Swap algorithms with a partner and follow them exactly. Mark any step which is not precise.
exit: Rewrite this to be precise: 'Make the sandwich.'
lessons.homework: Decompose a task you do at home (for example laying the table for iftar or dinner) into 4 parts and write an algorithm for one of them.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: provide a template with numbered boxes and picture prompts; allow pupils to record oral algorithms. Stretch: ask pupils to decompose a part into even smaller parts.

lessons.unit: Unit 1: Programming with sequence and repetition
lessons.title: Scratch: sprites, events and sequences
objectives: Use event blocks to start a program
Build a sequence of motion, looks and sound blocks
Predict, run and debug a short Scratch program

keywords.def: a character or object in a Scratch program
something that starts a script, such as clicking the green flag
a stack of blocks that make up a program

starter: Bismillah. Decomposition means breaking a ___ problem into ___ parts.
Put in order: open the lid, switch on the computer, press the button.
Why must an algorithm be precise?

teach.heading: Meet Scratch
bullets: The stage is where things happen.
teach.note: Share your screen with Scratch open. Point out the stage, sprite list, block palette and script area. Pupils need a free Scratch account or the offline editor; if using the browser editor with no account, remind them to save the file using File, Save to your computer.

teach.heading: Events start scripts
bullets: 'When green flag clicked' starts a script.
'When space key pressed' starts a script.
teach.note: Demonstrate a one-block script: when green flag clicked, move 10 steps. Click the flag several times; the sprite keeps moving. Emphasise that blocks run in order from top to bottom.

teach.heading: A greeting sequence
teach.note: Build this live and ask pupils to predict what will happen before you click the flag. Show how swapping two blocks changes the story. Link to the sunnah of greeting with salam first.

teach.heading: Debugging a script
teach.note: Show a buggy script where the sprite moves before it says hello when it should say first. Ask pupils how to fix it by swapping blocks. Model changing one thing at a time, so we know what fixed it.

practice: Predict: when green flag clicked, move 100 steps, say 'Hi!' for 1 second. Where does the sprite say 'Hi!'? (after moving)
Together, add a 'play sound' block and predict when the sound plays.
Which event block starts a script when you press the space bar?
independent: Open Scratch and make a sprite say 'Assalamu alaykum' then move across the stage and say its name.
Add a second sprite which replies 'Wa alaykumussalam' after a wait block of 2 seconds.
Stretch: change the backdrop when the sprites finish talking.
exit: Which block starts the script when the green flag is clicked?
lessons.homework: Practise at home: build a script of 5 blocks in Scratch that makes a sprite move, speak and change costume. Take a screenshot to share.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: provide a screenshot of the finished script to copy and a word bank for block names. Stretch: add a key-press event so the sprite does a different action.

lessons.unit: Unit 1: Programming with sequence and repetition
lessons.title: Repetition: loops in Scratch
objectives: Use the 'repeat' block to repeat actions
Explain why loops make programs shorter
Draw a square and a pattern using a loop

keywords.def: a block that repeats the instructions inside it
do the same steps a set number of times
an extension that draws lines as a sprite moves

starter: Bismillah. What does 'when green flag clicked' do?
Write the steps to clap 5 times using the word 'repeat'.

teach.heading: Why loops?
bullets: Move 10, turn 9 written forty times is long!
Loops save time and avoid mistakes.
teach.note: Show a script with the same two blocks copied twelve times. Ask what would happen if they made a mistake in one copy. Then show the same script using one repeat block. Pupils should see loops are shorter and easier to fix.

teach.heading: The repeat block
teach.note: Demonstrate dragging a move block inside and outside a repeat. Ask pupils where the sprite finishes in each case. Misconception: pupils think the number is the number of extra repeats; it is the total number of times.

teach.heading: Draw a square
teach.note: Add the Pen extension and build the script live. A square has 4 equal sides and 4 right angles. Ask: what would repeat 5 draw? Test the answer; pupils will see a missing line or an open shape, which leads to discussion.

teach.heading: Patterns with loops
bullets: Change the numbers to change the shape.
teach.note: Test the triangle and hexagon scripts live. Link to Islamic geometric patterns: many are built from repeated shapes, such as hexagons and stars. Encourage pupils to experiment with the angle and repeat numbers and explain what changes.

practice: How many sides does the shape have if the script is 'repeat 4: move 100, turn 90'? Predict, then test.
Debug: the sprite is meant to draw a square but turns 60 degrees each time. What should it be?
Write a loop that makes a sprite move 10 steps and say 'Allahu akbar' 3 times.
independent: Build the square script in Scratch and make it draw a square with sides of 80 steps.
Change the script to draw a triangle (3 sides, 120 degrees) and then a hexagon (6 sides, 60 degrees).
Stretch: put your square script inside a repeat 12 loop with a turn of 30 degrees after each square to make a pattern.
exit: What shape does 'repeat 3: move 100, turn 120' draw?
lessons.homework: Design a pattern on paper that uses a repeated shape. Write the loop you would need to draw it.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: provide a ready-made block set to assemble and label each block with a picture. Stretch: ask pupils to work out the turning angle for a pentagon (72 degrees) and test it.

lessons.unit: Unit 1: Programming with sequence and repetition
lessons.title: Project: an animated greeting card
objectives: Plan a short animation by decomposing it into scenes
Combine events, sequences and loops in one program
Test, debug and improve the program

keywords.def: pictures shown quickly one after another so they seem to move
run a program to check it works
change a program to make it better

starter: Bismillah. What does the 'repeat' block do?
Name two events that can start a Scratch script.
Why do we test our program after each small change?

teach.heading: The project
bullets: Make an animated Eid greeting card.
teach.note: Introduce the project and show a quick example: a star spins while the sprite says 'Eid Mubarak!'. Explain the success criteria and ask pupils to suggest extras. Remember that Eid cards and greetings are a joyful part of our culture.

teach.heading: Plan in parts
teach.note: Reuse decomposition from lesson 1. Pupils sketch three boxes on paper (storyboard) and write which blocks they will need. Check plans before they start building.

teach.heading: Build and test
bullets: Build one scene at a time.
teach.note: Walk round the breakout rooms or watch screens shared in Teams. Ask the question: what did you predict would happen? Highlight good debugging. Typical bugs: loops outside scripts, missing event block, sprite at wrong place.

teach.heading: Share and improve
bullets: Show your card to a partner.
Say one thing that works well.
teach.note: Model kind feedback: 'I like how... Next time you could...'. Link to sincere advice (nasihah) given with kindness. Give time for pupils to make one improvement.

practice: Plan on screen: which blocks would you use to make a star spin forever? (when flag clicked, forever, turn 15 degrees)
Which scene should be built first and why?
Find the bug: the message 'Eid Mubarak!' never appears because the say block is after a forever loop.
independent: Create your animated greeting card with at least 3 scenes, one sequence and one loop.
Test your program three times and write down one bug you fixed.
Present your card to a partner and give one improvement suggestion each.
exit: Name one bug you found and fixed today.
Which part of your program uses a loop?
lessons.homework: Add one more improvement to your card (a new backdrop or a new costume) and describe in one sentence what you changed.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: provide a template project with scenes set up and sentence starters for feedback. Stretch: ask pupils to add a click event so the viewer chooses the next scene.
